title: A Traceable Coding and Analysis Workflow
summary: After completing this intermediate module, a learner can turn an analysis question into a traceable workflow, validate its outputs, and document the evidence needed to review or repeat the work.
objectives: Define an analysis question, its intended decision, and the evidence that will count as a successful result.
Organize inputs, transformations, outputs, and checks so another person can trace how a result was produced.
Validate an analysis by checking assumptions, intermediate results, final outputs, and exceptional cases.
Document data provenance, processing decisions, evaluation procedures, limitations, and intended use.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The cited source record content/modules/ai-foundations/coding-and-analysis-workflow.json changed because it was a repository-relative path from an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. It has been replaced in the source list with canonical public records for the technical-debt, dataset-documentation, and model-reporting literature.

This correction affects citation provenance and the scope of the supported guidance. The workflow below is limited to practices supported by the replacement sources, including tracing data dependencies, documenting data and processing decisions, and recording evaluation procedures, limitations, and intended use.

sections.title: Level and starting point
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you can read a short program, identify its inputs and outputs, and interpret a basic table of results. It does not assume familiarity with a particular product, programming language, or provider.

The new capability developed here is workflow design. Instead of treating a successful run as sufficient, you will be able to assemble a reviewable chain from the original question through the data and transformations to validated outputs and documented limitations.

sections.title: Define the analysis contract
paragraphs: Begin by writing the question the analysis is intended to answer. Then identify who will use the result, what decision it informs, which inputs are in scope, what output is expected, and what evidence would make that output acceptable. This creates an analysis contract against which later work can be checked.

Record important exclusions and limitations before implementation. A result can be internally consistent while still being unsuitable for a decision that falls outside the stated purpose. Model Cards for Model Reporting supports documenting intended use, evaluation procedures, results, and limitations rather than presenting an output without context.

sections.title: Build a traceable flow
paragraphs: Organize the work as a sequence of inputs, transformations, intermediate results, checks, and final outputs. Preserve the identity and provenance of each input, and record any filtering, joining, recoding, aggregation, or exclusion that changes what the input represents.

Datasheets for Datasets proposes documenting why data was created, what it contains, how it was collected and processed, its intended uses, and how it is maintained. Applying those questions to an analysis makes hidden assumptions easier to find before they affect a conclusion.

Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems explains that data dependencies and surrounding system behavior can create complexity beyond the visible analytical code. A traceable workflow therefore records both the transformation logic and the dependencies that determine what reaches that logic.

sections.title: Validate before interpreting
paragraphs: Validation asks whether each stage behaved as intended, not merely whether execution completed. Check that required inputs are present, data types and ranges are plausible, exclusions follow the analysis contract, intermediate results retain the expected meaning, and final outputs satisfy the previously defined acceptance evidence.

Inspect exceptional cases rather than reviewing only typical or successful cases. Compare results with simple expectations derived from the question, and investigate discrepancies before interpreting the output. If a check fails, stop the interpretation and trace the result backward through transformations and inputs.

Keep evaluation procedures beside the results they produced. Record what was checked, why the check was relevant, what evidence was observed, and which limitations remain. This allows a reviewer to distinguish a supported result from an output that has merely been generated.

sections.title: Document for review and repetition
paragraphs: A reviewable analysis record identifies the question, intended decision, input provenance, processing decisions, validation evidence, final output, intended use, and known limitations. It should also make clear which decisions required judgment so that another person does not mistake them for unavoidable properties of the data.

Suppose an analysis counts records that meet a stated condition. A traceable workflow records the condition, identifies the input collection, preserves the original input, records exclusions and transformations, compares intermediate counts with expectations, inspects unusual records, and explains what the final count can and cannot support. A reviewer can then follow the result backward instead of trusting only the final value.
The workflow is complete when a reviewer can connect the conclusion to its evidence, locate each consequential transformation, understand the checks performed, and identify remaining limitations.

questions.prompt: What did the source correction affect?
choices: Citation provenance and the scope of the supported guidance
The addition of a required named product
questions.explanation: The previous repository-relative source record was replaced with canonical public records. The module states that this changes citation provenance and limits the guidance to practices supported by those replacement sources.

questions.prompt: What should be defined before implementing the analysis?
choices: Only the format of the final output
The question, intended decision, in-scope inputs, expected output, and acceptance evidence
Only the transformations that are easiest to perform
A conclusion to confirm with the available data
questions.explanation: The module calls this set of definitions the analysis contract. It provides a basis for checking the implementation and interpreting the result.

questions.prompt: Which action demonstrates validation rather than merely successful execution?
choices: Accepting the output because execution completed
Checking inputs, intermediate results, final outputs, and exceptional cases against stated expectations
Removing limitations from the analysis record
questions.explanation: Validation checks whether each stage behaved as intended and includes exceptional cases. Completion of execution alone does not establish that the result is suitable for interpretation.

questions.prompt: Which information belongs in a reviewable analysis record?
choices: Only the input collection and conclusion
The question, provenance, processing decisions, validation evidence, intended use, and limitations
Only the cases that support the conclusion
questions.explanation: The module identifies these elements as necessary for connecting a conclusion to its evidence and tracing consequential decisions.
